title: The Red and the Black, Stendhal
subject: litterature
description: Julien Sorel, son of a carpenter, wants to rise in a closed France. Stendhal invents the modern psychological novel.

hero.hook: Red for the uniform, black for the cassock: two colors, one ambition.

blocks.text: Published in **1830**, **The Red and the Black** is the birth certificate of the psychological novel, centered on the inner thoughts of the character. **Stendhal**, whose real name is **Henri Beyle**, follows **Julien Sorel**, a young commoner without a noble title, devoured by ambition in the , a period when the Bourbons returned to power after Napoleon. **[[The French Restoration (1815-1830)]]**

Between Napoleonic nostalgia and stifling society, the novel analyzes social hypocrisy and the torments of a soul searching for its place. Julien regrets the time when talent could be raised through the army. Stendhal lucidly describes how we calculate our feelings in order to move forward. Julien becomes the model of the modern romantic hero: intelligent, proud, but trapped by his time.

Stendhal boasts a dry style, influenced by his military career under Napoleon. He calls it : clarity, sincerity, refusal of romantic emphasis. For him, writing means coldly analyzing human passions. **[[Beylism]]**

blocks.caption: Stendhal: the implacable analyst of passions.

blocks.text: Stendhal read a few pages of the Civil Code every morning to keep his tone natural and devoid of emphasis.

The subtitle, , recalls the double ambition of the book: to paint the soul with precision and to paint the portrait of a sclerotic France, frozen and incapable of changing. The novel appeared shortly before the **Three Glorious**, the revolution of July 1830 which overthrew Charles X. **[[Chronicle of 1830]]**

sections.title: Julien Sorel: energy against the system

blocks.text: The despised son of a carpenter, Julien has a rare intelligence. He recites the , Latin translation of the Bible, in Latin. In **1830**, the “red” of the military uniform, the career under Napoleon, gave way to the “black” of ecclesiastical dress, the only vector of power for an educated commoner. **[[Vulgate]]**

blocks.caption: Restoration France: a society where ambition must be hidden.

blocks.text: Julien entered the seminary, a school for priests, then became a tutor at the **of Renal** in **Glass roofs**, in Franche-Comté. His conquest of **Mrs. de Rênal** is first and foremost a war operation, not a crush. Hypocrisy becomes his survival tool. The plot is inspired by the case of **Antoine Berthet**, seminarian sentenced to death in **1827**.

sections.title: From the provinces to Parisian salons

blocks.text: In Paris, Julien becomes secretary to the **Marquis of La Mole**, a great aristocrat. He seduces **Mathilde de La Mole**, a proud young woman who loves danger and scandal. Julien sees her as the ultimate trophy of his social ascension.

In Stendhal, love is often a staging where we observe ourselves more than we abandon ourselves. Julien obtains a title of nobility and the agreement to marry Mathilde, but a letter from **Mrs. de Rênal** denounces his lies. The  contrasts the military uniform with the ecclesiastical dress, the only levers of ascension for a commoner in this closed society. **[[The symbolism of Red and Black]]**

sections.title: The truth at the foot of the scaffold

blocks.text: Julien shoots Madame de Rênal in the church of Verrières, after she writes a compromising letter. In prison, he stops calculating. Faced with death, ambition fades in the face of regret for the happiness experienced with her. He refuses to save his head through intrigue or aristocratic protections. **Mathilde** carries her severed head in a theatrical gesture, true to her character. Stendhal thus shows that only the truth of feelings survives in social theater.

events.detail: The novel appeared shortly before the Three Glorious Years.

blocks.text: In **The Red and the Black**, published in **1830**, Stendhal shows how social ambition and sincere happiness are opposed in a society based on hypocrisy.
